KEYWORDS: zoledronic acid, Ewing sarcoma, primary bone tumor, osteoclast, osteoprotegerin.
Bisphosphonates have a profound effect on bone resorption and are widely used in the treatment of osteoporosis and other osteoclast-mediated bone diseases.

To understand why this class of drugs is so important, consider that bone is not static; it is constantly being remodeled. Osteoclasts break down old bone, and osteoblasts build new bone. Bisphosphonates work by interfering with the osteoclasts, slowing down the breakdown process.

Zoledronic acid (Zometa, Novartis, East Hanover, NJ) is a new generation of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates that have demonstrated potent inhibition of bone resorption and antitumor activity in vitro
$^{1-3}$ Recent studies have demonstrated the therapeutic benefits of bisphosphonates for metastatic bone tumors in patients with prostate cancer or breast cancer. $^{4-9}$
acid reduced the metastatic bone tumor and prevented skeletal
complications, such as fractures or severe pain.

However, the efficacy of zoledronic acid on primary bone tumors has not been investigated. The mechanism of its inhibition of bone tumor growth is also unclear at this

time. Ewing sarcoma is the second most common malignant bone tumor in children and young adults. In the past 15
the survival rates for relapsed patients have not changed, despite the use of intensive chemotherapy and radiation therapy. $^{10}$

This stagnation in clinical outcomes highlights a critical gap in current medical practice: existing treatments are effective for initial diagnosis but fail to prevent or manage recurrence effectively. Consequently, new
established a Ewing sarcoma primary bone tumor animal model

for the purpose of evaluating new therapies. Using this model, we demonstrated that zoledronic acid up-regulated osteoprotegerin (OPG) expression, inhibited osteoclast activity, and decreased bone tumor growth. These results may provide a new approach to treating Ewing sarcoma bone tumors.

Cell Lines
TC71 human Ewing sarcoma cells were cultured in Eagle's modified essential medium with 10% fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L-glutamine, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 1× nonessential amino acid, and 2× MEM vitamin solution (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY). Normal human osteoblast (HOB) cells were purchased from Cambrex (East Rutherford, NJ) and cultured in specific media according to the manufacturer's instructions. All cells were screened with a Mycoplasma Plus PCR Primer Set (Stratagene, La Jolla, CA) and found to be free of mycoplasma.

Bone Tumor Animal Model
TC71 cells in log-growth phase were harvested and resuspended in cold Hank's balanced salt solution at $2 \times 10^{7}$ cells/mL. Athymic nude mice, 4–5 weeks old, were purchased from Charles River Breeding Laboratories (Kingston, MA). The mice were maintained in an animal facility approved by the American Association for Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care and in accordance with current regulations and standards of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the National Institutes of Health. Animals were housed for 1 week before experiments were begun, then $2 \times 10^{5}$ TC71 cells were injected into the right tibia under anesthesia. Four days after tumor cell injection the mice were divided into groups and treated with zoledronic acid alone (200 $\mu$ g/kg, subcutaneously, twice weekly), paclitaxel (Taxol, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Princeton, NJ) alone (6 mg/kg, intraperitoneally, once a week), or zoledronic acid in combination with paclitaxel. Mice in the control group were treated with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The bone tumor size was measured after 5 weeks with the MX-20 Specimen Radiograph digital imaging system (Faxitron X-ray, Wheeling, IL). To determine the extent of bone destruction, the bone tumors were scored from 0–4 according to criteria previously described. $^{11}$ Grade 0 represented no bone lysis; Grade 1, minimal but visible bone lysis within the medullary canal; Grade 2, moderate bone lysis in the medullary canal with preservation of the cortex; Grade 3, severe bone lysis with cortical disruption; and Grade 4, massive destruction.

Cell Proliferation Assay
Five thousand cells were seeded onto 96-well cell culture plates and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were treated with different concentrations of zoledronic acid or paclitaxel alone or paclitaxel plus 10 $\mu$ M zoledronic acid. The antiproliferative activity was determined by the 3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl]-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide thiazolyl blue (MTT) assay as described previously. $^{12}$

Annexin V Assay
Apoptosis induced by zoledronic acid was quantified using the Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Calbiochem, La Jolla, CA). TC71 cells were treated with PBS (control), 30 $\mu$ M of zoledronic acid, 1 $\mu$ M of paclitaxel, or both drugs together for 24 hours. Cells were trypsinized and counted, then 5 × 10 $^{5}$ cells in 0.5 mL were incubated with 1.25 $\mu$ L Annexin V-FITC at room temperature for 15 minutes in the dark. After centrifugation at 1000g for 5 minutes, the media were aspirated, the cells resuspended in cold binding buffer, and 10 $\mu$ L propidium iodide was added. The apoptotic cells were analyzed by flow cytometry.

Having established that zoledronic acid is effective in vivo, we must now ask: *how* does it work? To explore a potential mechanism by which zoledronic acid inhibited the osteolytic (bone-destroying) activity of tumor cells, we determined the effect of zoledronic acid on osteoclast formation in the TC71 tumors using TRAP staining.

**Key Concept: Osteoclasts and TRAP Staining**
Before proceeding, it is crucial to understand the players involved. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells responsible for breaking down bone tissue. In the context of bone tumors, their excessive activity leads to the "osteolytic" damage observed in the previous section. To visualize these cells, researchers use Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase (TRAP) staining. Think of TRAP staining as a specific highlighter that marks osteoclasts, allowing them to be identified as the distinctive multinuclear purple-staining cells in the bone tissue (indicated by the arrow in Fig. 3).

The number of osteoclasts was significantly decreased in animals treated with zoledronic acid

(Fig. 3B) compared with untreated tumor (Fig. 3A). The quantitative data show (Fig. 3, bottom) that the average osteoclast number per microscope field (mean number from counting 5 random microscope fields) is 18 in untreated bone tumor, reduced to 7 in zoledronic acid-treated bone tumor. These data indicate that zoledronic acid inhibited osteoclast formation in Ewing sarcoma bone tumor. The decreased bone damage in zoledronic acid-treated animals was secondary to the drug's effect on osteoclasts.

RANK/RANKL/OPG Pathway: A Simplified Model**
Imagine this pathway as a communication system between cells. RANKL acts as a "signal" that tells osteoclasts to form and become active. RANK is the "receiver" on the osteoclasts. OPG (Osteoprotegerin) acts as a "decoy" or shield; it binds to RANKL, preventing it from reaching RANK, thereby stopping the signal for bone destruction. If zoledronic acid is effective, we might expect it to boost the production of this protective shield, OPG.

DISCUSSION
A number of studies have demonstrated the beneficial effects of bisphosphonates on bone metastases from different solid tumors, including breast, prostate, and renal cell carcinoma. $^{13,14}$
effect of bisphosphonates on primary bone
originate directly in the bone rather than spreading from elsewhere—has
To address this gap in knowledge, we

established a primary Ewing sarcoma animal model in nude mice. Using this model, we now demonstrate that zoledronic acid significantly inhibits osteolytic Ewing sarcoma growth in vivo and enhances tumor sensitivity to paclitaxel (Fig. 2). Our in vitro data suggest that zoledronic acid has a direct effect on tumor cells, as it inhibited tumor cell proliferation and induced apoptosis (Fig. 1).

In addition to its direct effect on tumor cells, our data indicate that other mechanisms are involved in zoledronic acid's efficacy in vivo. Ewing sarcoma is a
1718
CANCER October 15, 2005 / Volume 104 / Number 8

lytic bone tumor, creating a “moth-eaten” appearance to the bone as it invades the normal bone cortex and destroys bone tissue (Fig. 2).

To understand this visual description, imagine a piece of wood being eaten away by termites; the surface becomes riddled with holes and irregularities rather than smooth and solid. In medical imaging, this "moth-eaten" look is a hallmark of aggressive bone destruction.
Osteolytic tumors are usually associated with enhanced osteoclast activity.

Here, it is crucial to understand the role of osteoclasts. These are specialized cells responsible for bone resorption—the process of breaking down bone tissue. Think of them as the "demolition crew" of the skeletal system. In a healthy bone, there is a balance between osteoclasts (demolition) and osteoblasts (construction). However, in the presence of an osteolytic tumor, the demolition crew goes into overdrive, rapidly clearing away bone mass to make room for the tumor.
TRAP staining showed a significant reduction in the number of osteoclasts in bone tumor tissue from mice treated with zoledronic acid (Fig. 3).

TRAP (Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase) is a specific enzyme found in mature osteoclasts, making it a reliable marker for identifying these cells under a microscope. The finding here is pivotal: zoledronic acid, a potent bisphosphonate drug, significantly lowered the number of these destructive cells.
Therefore, decreased osteoclast activity may play a role in zoledronic acid’s efficacy, as well as its alteration of the phenotype of the tumor.

This suggests that the drug doesn't just kill the tumor cells directly; it also disrupts the tumor's ability to destroy bone, effectively changing the tumor's behavior (phenotype) from a bone-destroying entity to one that is less destructive.
Mechanisms involved in decreasing osteoclast activity by zoledronic acid were also investigated.
To understand how the drug works, we must look at the molecular signals that control osteoclast formation.
RANKL has been shown to be critical to osteoclast formation.

RANKL (Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Ligand) acts as the "on switch" for osteoclasts. It binds to a receptor called RANK on the surface of osteoclast precursors, triggering their differentiation into active, bone-resorbing cells.
We were unable, however, to demonstrate a change in either RANK or RANKL following treatment with zoledronic acid.
This is a critical negative result. It tells us that the drug is *not* working by simply turning off the "on switch" (RANKL) or removing the "receptor" (RANK).
Zoledronic acid did not inhibit RANK expression or affect the ratio of RANK/RANKL.
Since the primary signaling molecules remained unchanged, we must look elsewhere for the mechanism of action.
also plays an important role in the regulation of osteoclast activity, and OPG is a decoy receptor for RANK.

If RANKL is the key, OPG is the lock that prevents the key from turning. OPG floats in the extracellular space and binds to RANKL, physically blocking it from reaching the RANK receptor on the osteoclast.
Increased OPG interferes with the binding of RANKL to the RANK receptor, resulting in the inhibition of osteoclast activity.
This is a classic example of competitive inhibition.
The RANKL/OPG ratio is important in the regulation of bone formation. Higher ratios or amounts of RANKL to OPG are associated with increased osteoclast activity.
Conversely, a lower ratio (more OPG relative to RANKL) means less osteoclast activity and less bone resorption.
Our data indicate that zoledronic acid up-regulated OPG expression, resulting in increased OPG protein production (Figs. 4, 5). This
is the breakthrough finding. The drug stimulates the production of the "decoy" receptor. This
would in turn lead to a decrease in the RANKL/OPG ratio and decreased osteoclast activity.

By increasing the amount of OPG, zoledronic acid ensures that more RANKL molecules are captured and neutralized before they can activate osteoclasts. This molecular shift explains the reduction in osteoclast numbers observed earlier.
The effect of zoledronic acid on the RANK/RANKL/OPG pathway varies depending on the tumor cell type.
It is important to note that biological systems are context-dependent.
Zoledronic acid has been shown to stimulate OPG but also to down-regulate RANKL in osteoblast-like cells. $^{15}$
This suggests that in different cellular environments, the drug might have multiple points of entry.

Therefore, the mechanisms involved for each specific tumor may be different. Other studies have shown that bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl diphosphonate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, in addition to its effect on the OPG pathway. $^{16,17}$

This highlights the multi-target nature of bisphosphonates. The mevalonate pathway is essential for cell survival and signaling; by inhibiting an enzyme in this pathway, the drug can have additional cytotoxic effects on the tumor cells themselves, independent of its effect on bone resorption.
In summary, we have demonstrated that zoledronic acid, one of the more potent bisphosphonates, inhibits the growth of Ewing sarcoma both in vitro and in vivo and alters the phenotype of the tumor.
This dual action—directly inhibiting tumor growth and modifying the tumor's interaction with bone—is significant.
Alteration of the lytic phenotype is most likely secondary to interference with osteoclast activity and subsequent bone resorption.
By blocking the osteoclasts via the OPG mechanism, the drug preserves bone integrity.
Zoledronic acid has been shown to have clinical activity against breast, prostate, and renal cell cancer bone metastasis, as well as having a role in preventing skeletal complications. $^{18-20}$
This establishes a strong precedent for its use in bone-related cancers.

Preclinical data also indicate that bisphosphonates may be effective against osteosarcoma. $^{21}$ Our data suggest that another primary bone tumor, Ewing sarcoma, may also be an appropriate tumor for therapeutic evaluation. Given the dearth of effective agents for treating patients with Ewing sarcoma, particularly those with relapsed disease, and the dismal 2-year metastasis-free survival, extending the application of zoledronic acid to include Ewing sarcoma warrants further evaluation.
This conclusion bridges the gap between preclinical success and clinical need, highlighting a potential new avenue for treating a currently difficult-to-manage cancer.
